body.rationale:
This is CVaR minimisation at a different setting, not the unconstrained method. The default, the pure minimum-CVaR portfolio, is essentially a cash fund: 0.62% volatility and a Sharpe of 0.05, far below the IPS 8% floor. The minimum expected return was raised to 8.219%, annualised from the historical scenarios, to walk Rockafellar and Uryasev's own mean-CVaR frontier up to 8.00% volatility. That setting is what produced a portfolio with real risk assets. It is a point on the same frontier, so a reviewer should judge it as the lowest 95% expected-shortfall portfolio that earns that historical mean. It is not a separate method.

The method reads no CMAs, so it carries none of the forecast error that return-optimised proposals inherit. In an expansion regime, with expected-return judgments that are neither clearly reliable nor clearly noisy, that is a real advantage. What it reads instead is the 1993-onward scenario set: fat tails, asymmetry and equity drawdowns count directly, which a covariance matrix cannot capture. Given a return floor, it fills it with the cheapest tail risk it can find. Here that is equities for return, intermediate Treasuries as the equity-stress offset, and gold as a diversifier whose tail behaviour differs from equities. The result is a barbell of a few assets, not a spread across many. That is the optimiser working as designed, though not a sign of broad diversification.

The portfolio is compliant on the ex-ante limits (return, volatility, tracking error). The drawdown limit is a backtest measure the CRO will check, so I do not claim full IPS compliance. The IPS is ratified. Tracking error against the benchmark is 3.60%, a deliberate active bet and not benchmark-hugging. Sharpe of 0.34 is modest, and about 2.9 effective assets is concentrated. A reviewer should weigh it as a tail-aware, forecast-free anchor and not as the highest-Sharpe candidate.
body.notes: Key assumption: That the 1993-onward monthly scenarios are a fair sample of the tail behaviour to come, in particular that Treasuries and gold will offset equity losses the way they did in that sample, and that the historical mean used for the return target is a usable guide to future return. Main weakness: Concentration in a few assets: 4 of 18 held, 2.9 effective assets, with 45% in one equity sleeve. The portfolio is only as good as the historical co-movement of equities, Treasuries and gold. Any regime in which stocks and bonds fall together (an inflation or rate shock) is under-represented in the scenarios and would hit both main holdings at once. In addition, the 8.219% return target is set on historical means, which is itself an estimation-error channel the method otherwise avoids, and the tuning to the volatility band means the portfolio is no longer the method's natural minimum-tail solution. Preferred when: When return forecasts are judged unreliable and tail loss matters more than variance, for example when the investor is sensitive to drawdowns and the asset return distributions are visibly skewed or fat-tailed. It is also useful as a compliant ensemble ingredient that brings gold and an equity/Treasury barbell, which covariance-based methods (risk parity, inverse variance, HRP) under-weight or spread thin. It should beat the alternatives when the history in the scenario set is representative of the stresses ahead. Invalidated if: If the next stress is a joint equity and Treasury sell-off, or gold fails to hedge, the tail structure this portfolio relies on will not hold and the 95% shortfall it minimised will understate the real loss. Rising stock-bond correlation, or a regime shift that makes the 1993-onward sample unrepresentative, would also invalidate it. If the CRO's backtest drawdown breaches the IPS limit, or the CIO's ensemble already supplies a more diversified route to the same volatility with a higher Sharpe, this concentrated portfolio is the wrong choice.
